items.name: Morel mushroom (gucchi)
items.prabhava: Prized Himalayan wild mushroom — festive building food of Kashmiri and Himachali kitchens.
contraindications: must be thoroughly cooked (raw morels are toxic)
items.preparation: Soak dried morels, rinse the honeycomb well of grit, and always cook fully — never raw.

items.name: Ker (desert caper berry)
items.prabhava: Desert survival food of Rajasthan — karira appears in classical texts; intensely flavored berry pickled or cooked in the ker-sangri pair.
combinations: ker-sangri with buttermilk soak and generous oil
items.preparation: Soak in water or buttermilk to tame bitterness before cooking; classic dry desert sabzi with sangri.

items.name: Sangri (desert bean)
items.prabhava: Pods of the sacred khejri tree — protein-dense desert legume that grows where nothing else will.
combinations: ker-sangri with oil and spices (the fat is essential)
contraindications: vata excess (dry preparations without adequate oil)
items.preparation: Soak dried pods overnight, boil, then temper generously — desert cooking answers its dryness with oil.
provenance: Rajasthani tradition; shami in classical lists

items.name: Gunda (dried lasora)
items.prabhava: The mucilaginous 'phlegm berry' of classical texts — its very name (shleshmataka) marks the kapha-building slime that soothes dry tissues.
contraindications: the sticky pit needs removal before cooking
items.preparation: Soak dried berries, remove pits, and cook into sabzi or pickle; the mucilage is the point, not a flaw.

items.name: Mahua flower (fresh)
items.prabhava: Sugar-rich forest flower — staple energy food of central Indian tribal cuisine, eaten raw, cooked, or sun-dried.
combinations: cooked with sesame or peanut (tribal preparations)
contraindications: note: fermented mahua liquor is a separate, intoxicating use — food entry covers flowers only
items.preparation: Fresh flowers are washed and cooked into sweets or dried for storage; deeply sweet and building.

items.name: Mahua flower (dried)
items.prabhava: Sun-dried mahua concentrates the sugars — used like raisins or jaggery in tribal sweets and porridges.
items.preparation: Rinse and soak briefly, then stew or grind into sweets; treat as a dried-fruit sweetener.

items.name: Black soybean (bhatt)
items.prabhava: Kumaoni hill staple — iron-rich black soybean cooked into churkani and dubuk; the mountain winter protein.
combinations: bhatt ki churkani (iron-pan stew with rice flour)
roasted as snack with ghee and salt
items.preparation: Traditionally cooked in an iron kadhai, thickened with rice flour — slow cooking and jambu-herb tempering make it digestible.

items.name: Rhododendron juice (buransh)
items.prabhava: Spring squash of Himalayan rhododendron petals — the mountain cooler, traditionally taken in the hot months.
combinations: with a pinch of rock salt
contraindications: only Rhododendron arboreum petals are edible — other species are toxic; source prepared squash reputably
items.preparation: Dilute the petal squash with cool water; a spring-harvest tradition of Uttarakhand and Himachal.

items.name: Stinging nettle greens (sisnu)
items.prabhava: Wild mineral-dense green of the hills — the sting vanishes with cooking; traditional early-spring blood-and-iron food.
items.preparation: Handle with gloves, blanch or boil — heat neutralizes the sting completely; cook like spinach with fat.

items.name: Fiddlehead fern (lingda)
items.prabhava: Monsoon foraged fern coils of the hills — brief seasonal delicacy from Himachal to Assam.
combinations: stir-fried with garlic and local oil
contraindications: must be cooked thoroughly (raw ferns carry thermolabile toxins)
items.preparation: Wash the coils well, blanch, then sauté fully — never raw or undercooked.

items.name: Taro stem
combinations: cooked with sour (tamarind, dried mango) — essential against the itch
contraindications: must be cooked long with souring agents (calcium-oxalate itch when underdone)
items.preparation: Peel the stems' fibrous skin, cook long with tamarind or amchur; the sour is functional chemistry, not just taste.

items.name: Nendran banana
items.prabhava: Kerala's firm cooking banana — steamed for breakfast, fried as chips, and the base of the infant food 'nendran podi'.
combinations: steamed with grated coconut and ghee (puzhungiyathu)
viruddha: with milk in the same sitting (kadali rule)
items.preparation: Steam whole until the skin splits — the traditional breakfast; heavier than table bananas, so morning is its hour.

items.name: Joha rice
items.prabhava: Small-grained winter aromatic rice of Assam — prized for fragrance and gentleness; traditionally considered easy on digestion.
combinations: plain with dals and fish curries
contraindications: diabetes (portion control, as all white rice)
items.preparation: Cook like fine white rice with slightly less water; the aroma is the treasure — don't mask it.

items.name: Bhut jolokia (ghost chili)
items.prabhava: Among the hottest chilies on earth — in Northeast tradition a tiny smoked amount flavors an entire pot; a condiment measured in slivers.
combinations: a sliver in chutneys and pork-free bean stews
smoked, with fermented bamboo shoot (Naga style)
contraindications: handle with gloves — capsaicin burns skin and eyes
items.preparation: Use slivers, not pieces; a single chili seasons many meals. Dairy, not water, quenches its fire.
items.reviewNote: Predraft hint gave vata −1; authored +1 for consistency with red-chili entry (extreme pungency dries and disperses vata in any real quantity).

items.name: Gondhoraj lime
items.prabhava: The 'king of aroma' — Bengal's perfume lime, used more for its fragrance than its juice; a few drops and the zest transform dal-bhaat.
items.preparation: Add at the very end — heat kills the aroma; the leaf is used like kaffir lime leaf.
items.reviewNote: Predraft hint listed heating; authored cooling for consistency with dravya.lime convention (lime cooling / lemon heating). Expert to standardize citrus virya.

items.name: Kaji nemu (Assam lemon)
items.prabhava: Assam's elongated, intensely juicy lemon — served with every thali as digestive and vitamin-C staple.
combinations: juice in warm water on waking
items.preparation: Squeeze fresh at serving; a single fruit yields far more juice than common lemons.

items.name: Thekera (Assam garcinia)
items.prabhava: Assam's kokum-cousin — sun-dried garcinia slices that sour fish curries and summer sherbets while staying cooling.
items.preparation: Simmer a dried slice into curries and remove; gentler and cooler than tamarind.

items.name: Kachampuli vinegar
items.prabhava: Black garcinia extract of Coorg — a few drops give the signature dark sourness of pandi curry; intensely concentrated.
items.preparation: Add by the teaspoon at the end of cooking; taste as you go — its sourness is far denser than vinegar.

items.name: Sugarcane vinegar (sirka)
items.prabhava: The classical fermented sour (shukta) in its Indian form — cane juice fermented to vinegar; kindles agni, preserves pickles and onions.
items.preparation: Always diluted or as condiment; classical texts treat shukta as digestive in drops, aggravating in draughts.

items.name: Coconut vinegar
items.prabhava: Fermented coconut-sap vinegar of the Konkan and Kerala coasts — milder and slightly sweeter than cane sirka.
items.preparation: The gentlest of the Indian vinegars; use as sirka but expect a rounder sourness.

items.name: Jamun vinegar
items.prabhava: Vinegar of the astringent jamun fruit — folk tradition pairs it with sugar-balance regimens; the astringency tempers the usual vinegar heat.
combinations: in summer sherbets with black salt
contraindications: hypoglycemia with diabetes medication (traditional use overlaps)
items.preparation: Dilute a tablespoon in water; the jamun astringency makes it the most vata-friendly of the sirkas. No medicinal claims — traditional use only.
provenance: North Indian folk tradition; jambu + shukta lineage

items.name: Betel nut (supari)
items.prabhava: Classical tambula component chewed after meals for kapha and mouth-freshening — but modern evidence overrides tradition here: areca nut is a Group 1 human carcinogen.
combinations: historical tambula (paan) tradition — documented for cultural completeness
contraindications: oral and esophageal cancer risk (IARC Group 1 carcinogen) — habitual chewing strongly discouraged
not recommended for any regular use
items.preparation: Included as cultural-classical reference only. This app does not recommend consuming areca nut; the recommendation engine must never suggest it.
items.reviewNote: Engine exclusion required: classical status notwithstanding, modern carcinogenicity evidence is conclusive. Display with prominent health warning; never recommend.

items.name: Catechu (katha)
items.prabhava: Khadira heartwood extract — the classical astringent for mouth and skin; the red stain of paan and a pinch-dose oral tradition.
combinations: pinch in paan (with the caveats of that tradition)
items.preparation: Pinch doses only; food use is as a bitter-astringent accent, not a bulk ingredient.

items.name: Mukhwas (fennel mouth-freshener)
items.prabhava: The after-meal seed ritual of Indian tables — roasted fennel with sesame, dhania-dal and sometimes candy; digestion and fresh breath in a spoonful.
combinations: plain roasted blends over candied ones
items.preparation: Chew slowly after meals; prefer unsweetened roasted blends — the candy-coated versions turn a digestive into a dessert.

items.name: Tender tamarind leaf
items.prabhava: Spring's sour young tamarind shoots — Andhra and Telangana cook them into dals and chutneys before the leaves toughen.
items.preparation: Use only the tender pale shoots; cook briefly into dals — a fleeting spring sourness.
